2. Steroid‑exacerbated perioral dermatitis — common after topical steroids on the face, similar histologic features (perifollicular and perivascular lymphocytes ± neutrophils), can produce persistent erythema and scarring.
3. Rosacea (papulopustular or granulomatous subtype) — chronic central facial erythema with sebaceous gland–centered inflammation fits biopsy; absence of recalled pustules makes it less certain but still plausible.
4. Steroid‑induced acneiform eruption — topical steroids can produce follicular neutrophilic inflammation centered on sebaceous units and persistent erythema.
5. Chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (discoid lupus) — can cause scarring/atrophy on the face but is less likely because DIF was normal and biopsy lacked a classic interface dermatitis; include as lower‑probability alternative.

Recommended next steps to confirm and guide treatment (brief):
- Correlate with a detailed clinical exam to map lesion distribution (central face, perioral, eyelids) and look for telangiectasia, follicular papules/pustules, scale, and degree of atrophy/scarring.
- Consider repeat targeted punch biopsy including epidermal interface sections if lupus remains a concern and/or culture/PCR if infection suspected.
- Trial withdrawal/avoidance of topical steroids if not already stopped and consider stepped therapy for steroid‑withdrawal dermatitis/rosacea (topical calcineurin inhibitors or systemic tetracycline class antibiotics under supervision).
